item.title: Hackers hijack Egypt highway billboard and Malaysian screens to show porn
item.description:
A hacking group claiming responsibility for displaying pornographic footage on a roadside billboard in Egypt told The Cairo Report that it exploited a software vulnerability affecting digital advertising screens in several countries, exposing what it described as widespread security failures in commercially operated infrastructure.

The group, which operates a Telegram channel called ‘Leakers$’, said its members discovered thousands of exposed systems through an automated scan lasting approximately two hours, during which it identified Iraq, Malaysia, Brazil, and China among the countries where it said it gained access to display systems.

The account follows an incident Thursday, Oct. 29, when sexually explicit footage appeared on a large electronic billboard overlooking one of the busiest highways in the country, the 26 July Corridor in Giza, which connects Cairo with its western suburbs.

Videos circulated on social media showed the footage playing on the screen, prompting authorities to suspend advertising displays along the road and open an investigation.

The affected billboard is operated by Arabian United, an Egyptian-Saudi advertising venture established by United Media Services (UMS), Egypt’s intelligence-linked media conglomerate, and Saudi-listed Arabian Contracting Services Co.

In a statement Thursday evening, Egypt’s Interior Ministry attributed the incident to the hacking of an unnamed international advertising company’s website, saying the same footage had appeared on screens in several countries simultaneously.

The ministry did not identify the international company, the countries affected, or any suspects. It also gave no technical explanation of how the alleged website breach translated into control over roadside advertising displays.

The group’s account broadly supports the ministry’s description of an international incident but provides a different level of technical detail.

In an exchange with The Cairo Report, a person speaking on behalf of the group said its members had exploited a vulnerability in the software used to transmit content to LED displays, rather than targeting the Egyptian billboard individually.

“It was a genuine vulnerability in the software responsible for transmitting content to LED displays,” the person said. “After exploiting it, we gained access to display systems in several countries, not just Egypt, but also Malaysia, Brazil, China, and others.”

The person added that the infrastructure was not exclusive to Egypt and contained multiple security flaws, including weaknesses accessible through the system’s own pages and interfaces.

Asked whether the operation involved exploiting an unknown software vulnerability or merely accessing poorly protected equipment exposed to the public internet, the representative described a software flaw but did not provide enough technical evidence to establish the precise method.

According to the representative, the group located its targets through automated scanning rather than selecting particular companies or countries.

“The systems were identified through an automated and random scan,” they said, adding that several participants using the online pseudonyms Never, 19ylegal, CH and Nivex were involved in identifying thousands of exposed systems over approximately two hours.

The representative shared visual records captured during the incident and referred to material on the group’s public Telegram channel.

The channel’s address was visible on the pornographic material displayed on the Egyptian billboard, allowing The Cairo Report to trace it and contact its administrators.

In its initial public statement, the group said its objective was to expose security failures rather than demand payment or carry out a ransomware attack.

“Companies charge millions to build infrastructure across multiple countries and leave LED screens and billboard networks wide open on the internet without basic protection,” the statement said.

The group also rejected the idea that taking control of the screens required advanced technical capabilities.

“It wasn’t nearly as complex an operation as many might imagine,” its representative told The Cairo Report.

Perhaps most importantly, the intrusion raises questions about cybersecurity oversight at Arabian United, whose shareholders include one of the Egyptian state’s most politically influential media companies.

UMS, the media arm of Egypt’s General Intelligence Service, was established in 2016 and controls more than 40 companies across television, newspapers, digital media, entertainment, and advertising.

The billboard’s operator, Arabian United, however, was established in 2022 through a partnership between UMS and Arabian Contracting Services Co., one of Saudi Arabia’s largest outdoor advertising businesses.

According to the Saudi company’s 2025 annual report, its Egyptian subsidiary operates a network of 1,926 advertising billboards, including 239 digital installations, across Cairo, Giza, Alexandria and the North Coast.

The Saudi company holds a 49.99% ownership stake in Arabian United but exercises effective corporate control through its 57% representation on the board of directors, according to its March 2026 financial statements.

The company’s annual report also says it supervises, manages, and operates every stage of the advertising process in Egypt, from installing screens and securing advertising clients to displaying their content.

That division of responsibilities is significant because the Interior Ministry attributed the incident to an “international service provider” without identifying it or explaining its contractual relationship with the Egyptian operator.

When asked what the incident suggested about the security capabilities of an advertising business associated with Egyptian intelligence, the group’s representative said such institutional connections offered no guarantee against technical weaknesses.

“If infrastructure operated by a company linked to Egyptian intelligence can be compromised, it demonstrates that such connections do not necessarily translate into strong cybersecurity,” the representative said.

Obviously, the association with UMS does not establish that Egyptian intelligence agencies were responsible for administering the compromised systems. It does, however, place the incident within a security apparatus-linked commercial network that has expanded its presence across some of Egypt’s most heavily monitored public spaces.

Arabian United acknowledged the intrusion, saying an unknown party had gained unauthorized access to one of its advertising screens.

The company said it had immediately suspended the screen, was investigating the incident in coordination with authorities, and that it “remained committed to the highest security and operating standards.”

Earlier in the day, security sources told Al-Shorouk that investigators were “examining whether the footage resulted from an external intrusion or had been uploaded by someone responsible for operating the screen.”

The incident also exposes a gap between the government’s extensive regulation of roadside advertising content and the publicly disclosed safeguards governing the digital systems on which that advertising increasingly depends.

Under Law No. 208 of 2020, Egypt established the National Authority for the Regulation of Roadside Advertising, reporting to the prime minister. Its board includes representatives of the defense, interior, and transport ministries, among other government bodies.

The authority is responsible for setting standards governing roadside advertising, including requirements concerning “public order and morality.”

At a September 2025 meeting, prime minister Mostafa Madbouly emphasized the need to “regulate advertising on public roads,” particularly “compliance with Egyptian societal values and the protection of the urban landscape.”

Neither that regulatory framework nor the government’s latest statements explain what cybersecurity standards apply to remotely operated advertising networks, whether the affected operator had undergone a security assessment, or who bears responsibility for auditing third-party software connected to publicly visible screens.

The Interior Ministry said legal procedures had been initiated but did not specify whether the investigation would examine failures by the Egyptian operator or its contractors.

item.title: William Nordhaus has died
item.description:
William D. Nordhaus, Sterling Professor of Economics, Emeritus, whose influential work as an economist transformed a field and who won the 2018 Nobel Prize in Economics for his pioneering work on the economics of climate change, died on Oct. 30 following a battle with glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer. He was 85.

Nordhaus was also a central figure on the Yale campus for more than 50 years, teaching generations of undergraduate and graduate students and holding key administrative roles for the university, including as provost and vice president for finance and administration.

His influential work ranged widely, from the economics of climate change to the measurement of technological change, the interaction of the business cycle and the election cycle, and the measurement of economic welfare — farsighted work done jointly with the late James Tobin, himself a Yale Nobel laureate and one of the most influential economists of his day.

Nordhaus is best known, however, for receiving the 2018 Nobel Prize for “integrating climate change into long-run macroeconomic analysis,” an achievement most prominently reflected in what was known as the DICE (Dynamic Integrated Climate-Economy) model, an influential model that examines the interactions among carbon emissions, climate change, and economic growth.

The DICE model helps policymakers estimate the economic costs of climate change, including such impacts as crop losses and rising sea levels, and weigh them against the costs of reducing emissions. Nordhaus used the model to demonstrate that a carbon tax can reduce emissions efficiently and to estimate the optimal level of such a tax, providing an influential economic framework for carbon pricing.

“The signal contribution of economics,” Nordhaus said in his Nobel speech, “is to recognize that climate change is a harmful unintended side effect of economic growth. The best remedy for such externalities is a pollution charge or what is now known as a carbon tax.”

He was curious about everything, deepening our understanding of everything he touched, from climate change and the business cycle to calculating the present value of Yale tuition from 1701 to the present.

Nordhaus began contemplating the economics of climate change in the 1970s, when few economists — or anyone else — were thinking about or studying it. The DICE model that he developed — together with his dozens of articles, worldwide lectures, and numerous books — paved the way for a vast body of research which continues to frame the ongoing debate on how best to address the threat of climate change.

Along the way, Nordhaus served his field and the nation: as an editor of scientific journals, a member of the Congressional Budget Office Panel of Economic Experts, the first chairman of the Advisory Committee for the Bureau of Economic Analysis, a chairman of the Board of Directors of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, and as a member of the President’s Council of Economic Advisers. He was a member of the National Academy of Sciences and a distinguished fellow and president of the American Economic Association.

Not to be ignored among his extraordinary accomplishments is his co-authorship of multiple edits of the textbook “Economics.” The textbook, first published in 1948 by economist Paul Samuelson, the first American to win the Nobel Prize in economics, remains the standard-bearer for the principles of economics courses nationwide. Nordhaus became co-author in 1985 and continued as the primary author, revising and updating it after Samuelson’s 2009 death, and maintaining it through its most recent 19th edition. In recent years he was working on a project through Lighthouse Books to make an economics textbook freely available to all learners.

William Nordhaus was born in Albuquerque, New Mexico, where his family gained prominence for its many civic contributions. His father, a Yale College and Yale Law School graduate, made his law firm one of the nation’s most prominent advocates of Indian law, focusing on the representation of American Indian tribes, tribal corporations, and Native American organizations; in 1984 his firm won a landmark water case for the Jicarilla Apache Nation. He also pioneered skiing in New Mexico’s Sandia Mountains and founded what became the Sandia Peak Ski Area, located in the Cibola National Forest. The younger Nordhaus remained a skier all his life.

Nordhaus arrived at Yale as an undergraduate in 1959, an event that he called “one of the great windfalls of my life”; he described Yale as a “paradise for minds coming to the age of abstract reason.” He took Directed Studies (DS), an intensive program for first-year students, and was taught by professors Vincent Scully, Leonard Krieger, Victor Brombert, and Richard Bernstein. These scholar-teachers, Nordhaus would say, “were role models for his future academic life.” He went on to graduate school at MIT, another place he thought of as a kind of paradise – he called it “Arcadia.” He was mentored there by Nobel laureates Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow, and his class was filled with young economists who would also become leaders of their generation.

Hired as an assistant professor at Yale right after completing graduate school, Nordhaus from the start on was involved in university affairs. The opposite of an insular scholar, he was an important figure in his department and on campus, teaching undergraduates as well as graduate students and appearing regularly at Connecticut Hall faculty meetings. When a Faculty of Arts and Sciences faculty senate was established, in 2015, he was one of its inaugural members and later its chair.

As an economist and as a university citizen, Bill Nordhaus pursued the truth with rigor and purpose.

In his two years as university provost, between 1986 and 1988, and later filling in as vice president for finance and administration in 1992-1993, he helped guide Yale through periods of financial volatility and structural reorganization, focusing on balancing the university budget and implementing long-term financial modeling. In 2014 he helped architect Yale’s internal carbon charge system — making Yale one of the first major universities to test institutional mechanisms for carbon pricing on its own campus.

“Bill was a great joy to have as a colleague and friend,” said William Brainard, Arthur Okun Professor of Economics, Emeritus, and Nordhaus’ close colleague and friend for 60 years. “He was curious about everything, deepening our understanding of everything he touched, from climate change and the business cycle to calculating the present value of Yale tuition from 1701 to the present.”

Over the years, Nordhaus was a trusted counselor to many university leaders and authored numerous institutional studies and reports. He and Bill Brainard, also a former provost, were affectionately known familiarly around campus as “The Bills.” When people wanted to strengthen their position on a contested issue, they might invoke “The Bills,” knowing the weight that their opinions carried as thoughtful, careful stewards of Yale’s legacy.

Nordhaus was a Yalie through and through: undergraduate, alumnus, faculty member, teacher, scholar, administrator, who in his contributions represented the best of what a university stands for. He had always loved and admired his Yale teachers. Their influence was evident in how he lived his own Yale life.

For years, he taught a large introductory lecture course in macroeconomics. An iconic photo (below) captured students from that class presenting Nordhaus with flowers on the day he won the Nobel Prize in October 2018.

“As an economist and as a university citizen, Bill Nordhaus pursued the truth with rigor and purpose,” said President Emeritus Richard Levin, Nordhaus’s student, friend, and colleague for over 50 years. “His devotion to Yale and his determined effort to understand the economics of climate change were two sides of the same coin. He wanted to perfect the institution he loved, and he wanted to spare humanity the avoidable harm of uncontrolled global warming.”

Nordhaus is survived by his wife, Barbara, a graduate of the Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis, a practicing psychoanalyst, and an assistant clinical professor at the Yale Child Study Center for many years; three children, Jeff, Monica ’91, and Rebecca ’95 (William Curry); and three grandchildren, Annabel, Margot, and Alexandra. Funeral arrangements are private and a memorial service will be held in the future.

It's the memory latency, stupid

Making GROUP BY faster by doing more (CPU!) work

When you see your databases CPU at 100%, what is it actually doing? We like to act as though CPUs run code linearly for simplicity's sake, but in truth CPUs are incredibly complex beasts; they can potentially do many instructions at once, or sometimes none at all (despite our console showing 100%). Because CPUs can do so many things, one CPU at 100% may be doing much less than another at 100%. A CPU is considered "idle" only if no task (Linux task) needs CPU time; this does not mean the CPU itself is being fully saturated. So why would a CPU not be fully utilized, even if it appears to be at 100%?

The answer is usually memory.

Memory accesses are orders of magnitude slower than internal CPU operations. To give a good picture of how much so, a modern CPU might be able to process somewhere in the realm of 4-8 instructions per nanosecond. A memory access to RAM can take somewhere in the realm of 50-100ns. To ease your mathing, that means a modern CPU can do around 400-800 instructions for every one memory access from RAM.

Given this, CPUs are built from the ground up to work their way around this. The most obvious way this is dealt with is CPU caches. CPU caches keep memory closer to the CPU than RAM, literally baked into the CPU chip. The closest cache (the L1 cache) takes around 1ns per memory operation- that's 50-100x faster than RAM! The "problem" here of course is that the CPU caches are fairly small; the L1 cache for a modern CPU is probably around ~64KB, while the farther caches max out at a few hundred MB for top end processors. A good database tries manipulating data in small "chunks" to take full advantage of caches, and you'll often hear cache utilization as being one of the top concerns of performance engineering.

Let's look at GROUP BY aggregations to get a better grip on cache utilization. In GROUP BY, we're looking to take a dataset, group it by a certain column (or more), and perform certain aggregations (for example, count, or sum on another column). The "naive" method might be to open a HashTable keyed by the group key that grows ever larger. For every new row, you would check if that key exists- if it does, go to it's corresponding aggregation and update the result. Simple, right? The problem is that if you have millions of unique groups, you're not utilizing your cache at all! Nearly every HashTable access will be a "cold" hit that goes to RAM. This means that although your CPU may /look/ like it's 100% utilized, in truth it'll constantly be waiting for cold memory accesses.

To demonstrate this, we'll take our state-of-the-art Pivot engine and ravage it! We'll remove all our complex logic and replace it with simplicity:

fn consume( &mut self, batch: RecordBatch, _sender: &mut dyn Sender<RecordBatch>, ) -> unary::Result<()> { let group_keys = batch.column(self.key_column).as_primitive::<Int64Type>(); for &key in group_keys.values() { // If the Group Key doesn't exist- set it to 0 // Afterwards, add 1 to the group- this will give us a count(*) GROUP BY key_column *self.counts.entry(key).or_insert(0) += 1; } }

We'll then run a simple query SELECT count(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID on the "hits" dataset ClickBench provides (99m rows). This query will give us a count per UserID, meaning we'll have an entry in our HashMap per UserID- I'll give a spoiler here that there are ~17m unique UserID. Our performance checks will be on a bare metal server from our good friends over at CherryServers (AMD EPYC 9124 Genoa, 16 cores, 128 GB DDR5). We unfortunately can't use a common AWS/GCP machine because we want access to counters that aren't exposed there for security reasons (for example, we want to see how much memory is passing from DRAM controller to us). We'll confine ourselves to a single core, since this naive group by can't run on many cores.

To run it:

cat > config.yaml <<'EOF' server: bind: 127.0.0.1:5440 workers: 1 datastores: default: kind: pivotlake location: ./data default: true users: pivot: auth: method: trust EOF taskset -c 3 pivot server --config config.yaml & taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c '\timing on' -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"

This takes... a whopping 3.9 seconds. Is that good? Is that bad? Everything in this world is relative, or so they say. If we run the query again (without restarting the server), it takes 3.6s. The second run is the one we're more interested in- there's no disk involved as everything is already sitting in our page-cache.

You'll notice we did taskset -c. This pins the process to a given CPU; this will allow us to run perf stat on that CPU and see what's going on internally. We'll measure two metric groups- percentage of CPU slots stalling because of memory (and not doing anything in the meanwhile), and percentage of CPU slots actually retiring a micro-op:

sudo perf stat -C 3 -M backend_bound_memory,retiring -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"

and we get back this

Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 8364109137 ex_no_retire.load_not_complete # 50.1 % backend_bound_memory 38233214040 de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls 8977647849 ex_no_retire.not_complete 11861387798 ls_not_halted_cyc 11431618219 ex_ret_ops # 16.1 % retiring 11858248045 ls_not_halted_cyc 4.030148989 seconds time elapsed

This tells us that 50.1% of the time, the CPU couldn't do anything because it was stalling on memory! And only 16.1% of the time the CPU was actually retiring (aka doing) operations.

Another interesting stat to get is how many of our CPU memory loads are coming from DRAM (and not from caches):

sudo perf stat -C 3 -e ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"

And the result:

Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 76190837 ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near 3.996301634 seconds time elapsed

Every load is 64 bytes (the minimum amount you can bring, a cache line), so we can multiply by 64 to see we pulled 4.5GB during this query from DRAM on CPU loads (this is without any prefetching).

Let's now try to improve our algorithm to take advantage of the CPU caches. To do this, we'll use a method called radix partitioning. The idea is to split the merge into two distinct phases:

Phase 1: In this phase, we're simply going to separate the keys into 4096 different partitions (simply a Vec of SlabVecs- a SlabVec is a data structure similar to a Vec that is above memory that is already paged in. We don't use Vecs for raw memory in Pivot because it creates a lot of variance; not something for this blog post!). The partition will be decided by hashing the key and taking it's top 12 bits (2**12=4096).

fn consume( &mut self, batch: RecordBatch, _sender: &mut dyn Sender<RecordBatch>, ) -> unary::Result<()> { let keys = batch.column(self.key_column).as_primitive::<Int64Type>(); for &key in keys.values() { let hash = self.hasher.hash_one(key); // Since we want top 12 bits, we shift the hash (a u64) 52 bits to the right let partition = (hash >> 52) as usize; self.partitions[partition].push(&mut self.allocator, (hash, key)); } Ok(()) }UserIDhash(UserID)70x002A91F3â¦420x0007C4E2â¦130xFFF3B05Dâ¦70x002A91F3â¦50x001D6A88â¦420x0007C4E2â¦990x002E17B4â¦70x002A91F3â¦

â

hash >> 52, the first 3 hex digits

0x000FFFâ¦

0x001FFFâ¦

0x002FFFâ¦

0xFFFFFFâ¦

Phase 2: When all data has come through, go partition by partition, each time creating a HashMap, aggregating the partition into it, and then outputting it. This phase is very similar to our original algorithm, but we're going to use the hash from phase 1.

fn into_outputter(self) -> unary::Result<Option<Self::Outputter>> { let mut groups = Vec::new(); for rows in &self.partitions { let mut table: HashTable<(u64, i64, u64)> = HashTable::new(); // (hash, key, count) rows.for_each(|(hash, key)| { match table.entry(hash, |group| group.1 == key, |group| group.0) { Entry::Occupied(mut group) => group.get_mut().2 += 1, Entry::Vacant(slot) => { slot.insert((hash, key, 1)); } } }); groups.extend(table.into_iter().map(|(_, key, count)| (key, count))); } Ok(Some(Outputter::new(groups))) }

At first glance, this solution may seem rather odd. We're doing more operations here, not less! Every row, in both solutions, is hashed and sent into a HashMap. But in this solution, we're first pushing rows into seemingly meaningless vecs.

The key here (no pun intended) is to understand why we've done this; it's to make the aggregating HashMaps smaller. By dividing our group by into 4096 pieces, we've made our working HashMaps much likelier to fit into our CPU caches. Every time we do a lookup on our HashMap, our CPU is more likely to find the relevant memory sitting in it's caches, which saves a big chunk of time. But why trust me? Let's run it!

taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c '\timing on' -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"

And... Boom! 3.3 seconds, and then on second run 2.7 seconds! We've definitely made an improvement. But to really drive this point home, let's run perf again:

sudo perf stat -C 3 -M backend_bound_memory,retiring -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"

And our results:

Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 3790955223 ex_no_retire.load_not_complete # 23.5 % backend_bound_memory 20376118172 de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls 5442424751 ex_no_retire.not_complete 10083617764 ls_not_halted_cyc 19350459182 ex_ret_ops # 32.2 % retiring 10023435553 ls_not_halted_cyc 3.575992317 seconds time elapsed

Now we can see the picture has completely changed- 23.5% of the time is spent on waiting for memory (as opposed to 50% before), 32% for actually retiring operations. You may notice we're actually doing more work, not less- in this run, we did 19350459182 operations (the ex_ret_ops counter), whereas before the database did 11431618219 operations. This is worth it though, because as we said before- if we can translate cold DRAM accesses into CPU instructions, it's nearly always a good trade to make. In this case, we went down from 8364109137 CPU slots stalled because of memory to 3790955223.

To complete the picture and really see we're pulling less memory from the DRAM, let's again check how many our memory loads come from DRAM:

sudo perf stat -C 3 -e ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 25688280 ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near 3.009547012 seconds time elapsed

Whoo! That means that on demand we pulled 1.5GB from DRAM, instead of 4.5GB in the naive version.

That, of course, isn't the limit of how much we can utilize our CPU cache for GROUP BYs. And utilizing our CPU cache isn't the only way we can "hide" DRAM latency; another trick is prefetching memory to our cache before we need it, and yet another trick is creating algorithms that allow maximization of memory throughput- but that's not for this blog! We'll go into that in our next blog where we look at our /seemingly very weird/ implementation of JOIN probing.

For now, without explaining too much, I'll leave you with Pivot's speed for this query on a single core:

Time: 1848.353 ms (00:01.848)

and the amount of RAM we bring:

Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 14917958 ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near 2.182674864 seconds time elapsed

Which comes out to 954 MB.

Of course, Pivot knows to run in parallel on our 16 cores (where there are many other interesting cases), in which case it comes out to:

Time: 171.773 ms

nice :)

Try out Pivot if you want to have super speeds above parquets (OSS fun!), see you next time.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio on peaceful mode
item.description:
GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio

Previously: We got Claude Code playing Factorio, Towards beating Factorio autonomously, and Faketorio: an agent testbed

I got GPT-5.6 Sol, running in Codex with low thinking level, to complete a peaceful (i.e. no biters) Factorio run in 13.5 hours of game time:

A timelapse of the full run is available on YouTube.

Similar to my previous post, this run used a game manager to allow Sol/Codex to interact with the game via a small library (though in this run it was Python rather than Bash). The library allows the model to play the game programmatically while enforcing the same restrictions that human players face when using the GUI (e.g. reach of the player, fog of war).

Observing the run was fascinating: Sol exceeded my expectations in some areas while also showing clear weaknesses in others. I have the entire run recorded and am working on a commentary video, but in the meantime here’s a small timelapsed segment showing some parts of the factory:

Besides the screencast, my run manager also captured production statistics throughout the game. Here’s a chart of total resource production, annotated with science research milestones:

I had planned to terminate the run after blue science research, but Sol’s surprising effectiveness convinced me to keep it going. Unfortunately, the scaling issues I thought would occur in the blue science stage appeared later and slowed Sol’s relative progress significantly.

The rocket launch was only achieved through significant ‘manual’ effort on Sol’s part as it papered over its late-game failures to connect certain production systems by repeatedly ferrying supplies between areas of the factory.

Still, I was pleased with the improvement over previous attempts with GPT-5.5 which suffered from the model’s failures to use transport belts at all.

I’m optimistic about autonomous Factorio play as a medium for building intuition about the nature of model capabilities. In many ways playing Factorio is analogous to programming but with the benefit of being much more legible to casual observers, making it convenient for grounding discussion of model behaviors.

I look forward to testing other models and thinking levels, as well as non-peaceful runs. Stay tuned!

item.title: The Duty of a Scholar
item.description:
The Duty of a ScholarOn November 16th, 2004 — π years after arriving in Oxford — I submitted my doctoral thesis. My mind wasn't really on my thesis though; I was thinking about an issue I had noticed in recent Intel CPUs: The "Hyper-Threading" (simultaneous multithreading) feature they introduced in 2002 could leak information between execution threads via the cache state.

There was a joke at the time that although the National Security Agency had opened up in recent years and started taking their defensive role more seriously, the one aspect of cryptography which they would never discuss publicly was side channel attacks — and this itself constituted a side channel, revealing the importance they attributed to the field. Being active in computer security, and recognizing that the NSA knew a few things about the topic, my immediate priority was to determine whether the information leakage I had identified was sufficient to construct a practical cryptographic side channel. By mid-December I had a proof-of-concept exploit which stole enough bits of an RSA private key for the entire key to be reconstructed, and I turned my attention to the hard part of the problem: Quietly notifying security teams and working together to get the issue fixed before disclosing it publicly.

This became my occupation for the next six months. While my Oxonian contemporaries were making corrections to their theses and applying for jobs, I set those aside (much to the irritation of my supervisors): I had a responsibility, and it took priority over mere career considerations. As it turned out, being unemployed proved useful in early May, when Intel — rather irked by my impending publication — asked Yahoo to order me to withdraw the paper; Yahoo was very happy to reply that, unlike many FreeBSD developers, I was not in fact employed by them and they were not in a position to threaten to fire me. On May 13th, 2005, I presented my paper at BSDCan and published an advisory on the topic; advisories were published at the same time or soon thereafter by FreeBSD, NetBSD, Red Hat, SCO, and Ubuntu.

Anyone involved with open source software security will recognize the process of responsible disclosure (now widely called "coordinated disclosure", after some people in the industry struggled with the concept of responsibility), although the length of this particular process was unusual. If you find a security vulnerability, you shouldn't ignore it (or worse, sell it to bad actors); conversely, it's irresponsible to simply publish the vulnerability and hope that the good guys can fix it before the bad guys exploit it. Instead, you have a responsibility to identify who needs to know about the issue and to contact them — quietly — so they can get patches ready to distribute to their users the moment the issue becomes publicly known.

In this particular case, I was unusually able to put my life on hold: I was single, child-free, and, after defending my thesis and returning home to Canada, living rent-free in my (very tolerant) parents' basement. While I had some bills to cover — being a type 1 diabetic, I had to purchase insulin — living in Canada meant that I didn't need to worry about the risk of extraordinary costs from a hospital stay. Had I been living in the USA, I would have needed to prioritize seeking employment and medical insurance and likely would not have been able to discharge the duty which fate had thrust upon me.

Engineers, of course, are familiar with such duties: While the precise language varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, nearly all professional ethical codes include a requirement to act upon safety hazards regardless of whether any personal connection exists. Members of the IEEE commit, for example, "to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public..." without that duty being limited to hazards arising from projects employing the Engineer in question: The duty "to disclose promptly" vests in any Engineer who recognizes that the hazard exists. As with responsible disclosure of software security vulnerabilities, however, the subject matter of this duty is limited in scope: There is no duty to report if work is being done inefficiently. As a legal duty this would be reasonable; but as a moral duty, I feel it sets the bar too low.

Engineering codes also often set out a process of escalation: In the common case of a licensed Engineer becoming aware of a hazard in a project they are working on, in the first instance they should report their concerns to their employer; only if that fails to yield results should they take more direct steps. This is both efficient and practical: Reporting an issue to someone who fails to act upon it isn't necessarily sufficient to discharge a duty, but conversely reporting everything broadly risks drowning out the few items which truly need broad attention. I routinely apply this same principle; for example, in 2009 I discovered that the Amazon EC2 firewall broke Path MTU Discovery by default and reported it to Amazon; but by November 2012 I concluded that Amazon was not going to address the problem, so I took to my blog to advise Amazon customers on how to fix Path MTU Discovery for themselves. (As it happened, Amazon fixed the bug a short time later.) While this was in no way a safety or computer security concern, I felt that, knowing what I did, I had an ethical duty to share that knowledge to help people who were affected by the issue.

In the Star Trek: The Next Generation episode "The First Duty", the late Patrick Stewart, speaking as Jean-Luc Picard, delivers a memorable speech about truth:

The first duty of every Starfleet officer is to the truth, whether it's scientific truth or historical truth or personal truth! It is the guiding principle on which Starfleet is based! If you can't find it within yourself to stand up and tell the truth about what happened, you don't deserve to wear that uniform!

The duty described here is a duty to uncover and not conceal the truth; while I agree with this duty, I don't think it goes far enough. To me, the duty includes actively seeking out people to whom the truth should be told. To hide behind "nobody asked" is to fail to fulfill the duty.

Much ink has been spilled by philosophers about duty and ethics, and the German Enlightenment philosopher Fichte in particular had some interesting comments to make in the fourth of his 1794 lectures, Über die Bestimmung des Gelehrten — often translated as The Vocation of the Scholar, which inspired the title of this essay. Fichte argues that Scholars have a particular relationship to knowledge: A Scholar "possesses his Knowledge not for himself, but for society". It is not proper for a Scholar to hoard knowledge; rather, Scholars have a duty to impart their knowledge to others — in Fichte's somewhat exaggerated view, to act as "the Teacher of the human race". On the other hand, it is unnecessary and inappropriate to enter with everyone into the "deep inquiries which he himself has been obliged to undertake"; rather, a Scholar relies upon others' trust in the Scholar's honesty when conveying the particular knowledge which is needed. Fichte notes that "[t]he Scholar will never be tempted to bring men to the adoption of his convictions by coercion or the use of physical force [...] neither will he deceive them". Scholars are not Plato's philosopher-kings; their duty is to provide the requisite knowledge, not to enforce what is done with that knowledge.

Now, I don't agree with Fichte on every point. Fichte considers Scholars to be the loftiest of all classes, and even invites each Scholar to consider themselves a "Priest of Truth"; living in rather more egalitarian times, I absolutely reject this framing. Nor do I accept Fichte's framing (in his preceding lecture, On the Distinction of Classes in Society) that the duty of Scholars to share knowledge arises from an obligation to render back to society what it has done for us; to me, the duty arises not from a debt to society, but rather attaches to knowledge itself, no matter who holds it.

This duty, naturally, is not unlimited. As Fichte notes, there is no duty to force people to act upon shared knowledge — indeed there is a moral obligation to accept everyone's freedom to choose how they act. Similarly, there is no duty to become a Cassandra: As with any gift, people are free to refuse the gift of knowledge, however unwise that might be; ultimately, if everyone who is able to act upon some knowledge has been made aware of it, the duty has been exhausted.

In modern vernacular, the terms "Scholar" and "Researcher" often overlap, but to me there is a very precise distinction: Researchers create new knowledge, while Scholars carry that knowledge to the people who need it — a narrower definition than that of Fichte, whose Scholars also carry a duty to strive to extend knowledge. Many people, of course, are both Researchers and Scholars; but there are plenty of people who perform research and publish papers without truly communicating their discoveries. The research paper which is published in a journal but never read is almost a cliché; but even papers which are read do not necessarily have the impact they deserve if they are read only by academics and not by anyone in a position to act upon the findings published. My undergraduate alma mater, Simon Fraser University — of which I have been a sitting Senator for over two decades — describes itself as "Canada's engaged university" and makes a point of valuing not just academic output but the work of connecting academic learning with the real world. A true Scholar, in my mind, is someone who feels bound by the duty of knowledge: To find the people with whom it should be shared.

It is for everyone to choose their own role in society, and not everyone feels every duty the same way; for that matter, just as my experience in 2005 would have been different had I needed to obtain medical insurance, not everyone is able to act upon a duty, no matter how much they feel it. But for myself, I choose the life and duty of a Scholar.

item.title: TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8
item.description:
Overview

Linux's stable kernels shipped a fix on October 11 and 15, 2026 for CVE-2026-98432, a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake that a remote, unauthenticated peer can reach. The kernel's own CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8, Critical. The fixed releases are 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10, and 7.3, and the bug goes back to Linux 4.4. The upstream fix is a four-line change, but most servers run a distribution's kernel, and as of 8:00 PM CDT, October 29, Ubuntu's tracker still reads "Vulnerable" for its kernel on every release, and Red Hat lists RHEL 8, 9, and 10 as affected with no fix.

Why it's urgent: the bug sits in code every Linux server runs when it accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, before any application sees the connection. Anthropic, whose researcher reported it, says its Claude model wrote a working proof-of-concept exploit that runs commands as root on "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener," with no credentials. See the timeline.

Key facts Field Detail CVE CVE-2026-98432, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," issued by the Linux kernel CNA Severity Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), the kernel CNA's score. Red Hat rates it Important with CVSS 3.1 8.1 (AC:H), SUSE rates it important, Ubuntu rates it High, and Oracle and Amazon rate it Important with CVSS 3.1 8.1. Weakness Use-after-free of IPv4 option data during the TCP handshake (the record lists no CWE) Impact Per the CNA's scoring notes: kernel heap contents disclosed to the remote peer, kernel memory corruption, or a crash. Red Hat: "primarily results in a system crash leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) or potential memory corruption." Fixed in 7.2.10 and 6.18.56 (Oct 11) · 6.12.113, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 5.15.223, and 5.10.272 (Oct 15) · 7.3 (Oct 18) No fix yet Ubuntu (every release), RHEL 8, 9, and 10, Amazon Linux 2, and Amazon Linux 2023's default kernel, as of 8:00 PM CDT, October 29. Upstream branches that reached end-of-life before 5.10 get no fix. Proof of concept Anthropic says Claude built a remote root exploit for servers with a multipath TCP listener. It hasn't published the exploit. CVE records Published on cve.org on October 15. NVD lists it as "Received," with no analysis of its own, as of 8:00 PM CDT, October 29. Credit Reported by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic. Fixed by Eric Dumazet and reviewed by Kuniyuki Iwashima, per the fix commit.
Who is affected

Any Linux kernel from 4.4 on that lacks the fix, whether it serves the network directly or hosts containers: a container runs on the host's kernel, so a new image doesn't change anything. IPv6 connections aren't affected by the main issue; the commit says "IPv6 is not affected by the first issue."

Release line Status on Oct 29, 2026 Fixed in Released 7.3 Mainline 7.3 (from 7.3-rc7) Oct 18, 2026 7.2 Stable 7.2.10 Oct 11, 2026 6.18 Longterm 6.18.56 Oct 11, 2026 6.12 Longterm 6.12.113 Oct 15, 2026 6.6 Longterm 6.6.159 Oct 15, 2026 6.1 Longterm 6.1.190 Oct 15, 2026 5.15 Longterm 5.15.223 Oct 15, 2026 5.10 Longterm 5.10.272 Oct 15, 2026 4.4 – 5.4 End-of-life upstream distro fixes only —
Distribution status

Distribution kernels carry backported fixes under their own version numbers, so check the tracker, not the upstream number. As of 8:00 PM CDT, October 29:

Ubuntu: the tracker lists the linux package as "Vulnerable" on every release. On 26.10, 26.04, 24.04, and 22.04 it adds "work in progress" in 7.3.0-10.10, 7.0.0-43.43, 6.8.0-149.149, and 5.15.0-203.213; 20.04, 18.04, and 16.04 show only "Vulnerable." Many cloud and hardware-enablement kernels are listed the same way, and no Ubuntu Security Notice has been published. Red Hat: RHEL 8, 9, and 10 and OpenShift Container Platform 4 are listed as affected, with no fix; RHEL 6 and 7 aren't affected (CVE page). Red Hat says mitigation "is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria." Debian: fixed in 12 "bookworm" (6.1.190-1, DLA-4841-1, and linux-6.12 6.12.113-1~deb12u1, DLA-4850-1), 13 "trixie" (6.12.113-1, DSA-6568-1), and unstable (tracker). SUSE: rated important. SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 (kernel-default 6.12.0-160000.40.1) and the 15 SP4, SP5, and SP6 LTSS kernels are fixed; 15 SP7 is in progress, and openSUSE Leap 15.6 and 16.0 are listed as affected (CVE page). Oracle Linux: rated Important, CVSS 3.1 8.1. Unbreakable Enterprise Kernel (UEK) errata for Oracle Linux 7, 8, 9, and 10 came out October 16: ELSA-2026-500397, ELSA-2026-500398, and ELSA-2026-500399 (CVE page). The page lists only the UEK kernels. Amazon Linux: rated Important, CVSS 3.1 8.1. On Amazon Linux 2023, kernel6.18 is fixed (ALAS2023-2026-3251, October 24) and kernel6.12 is fixed (ALAS2023-2026-3335, October 29). The default kernel package and every Amazon Linux 2 kernel are "Pending Fix" (CVE page). How the vulnerability works

When a Linux server accepts a TCP connection, the kernel tracks the half-open handshake in a lightweight "request socket," then creates a full socket once the handshake completes. If the connecting peer's IPv4 header carried options, the kernel keeps them to echo in its replies. The bug: the kernel handed those saved options from the request socket to the new connection without copying them, then freed them immediately when the connection went away, while another CPU could still be reading them to build a handshake reply. Reading freed kernel memory is a use-after-free.

The peer needs no login, and it all happens inside the kernel's handshake handling, before any application code runs. The CNA's scoring notes say the stale data can leak kernel heap memory back to the peer, steer kernel writes out of bounds, or crash the machine. Anthropic says a lost race "only fails the handshake without crashing the whole system, so a determined attacker can retry indefinitely until they succeed."

The fix

Eric Dumazet's commit, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," changes two plain kfree() calls to kfree_rcu(), which waits until every reader has finished with the memory before freeing it. Other code paths that replace these options already did that. The commit also fixes the same problem in request-socket migration (net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1, or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE program), and says a related IPv6 case "will be addressed in a separate patch."

Which servers are exposed Every Linux host that accepts IPv4 TCP connections on an affected kernel: web servers, SSH, databases, load balancers, and Kubernetes nodes. The CNA's notes say the vulnerable path runs "during the TCP handshake, before application authentication." Hosts with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener first. That's the setup Anthropic's working exploit needs: "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener." Anthropic hasn't said why that listener matters, and the CVE record doesn't mention MPTCP. A server has one only if an application opens an MPTCP socket; the check is below.

Red Hat rates the bug lower than the CNA. It scores the attack complexity as High (CVSS 8.1) and describes the result as mainly a crash "or potential memory corruption." Anthropic's lab exploit shows a remote root shell on at least one configuration, so a lower rating isn't a reason to wait.

How to check your systems Check the kernel

Compare the result with your distribution's status above, not with the upstream version. If the installed kernel is newer than the running one, the fix isn't active until you reboot. Run these on container hosts and Kubernetes nodes, not inside containers: a container reports the host's kernel. We ran them on a Debian 12 host and in a Rocky Linux 9 container.

Check for multipath TCP listeners

ss -M lists only MPTCP sockets, so an empty result means no MPTCP listener. net.mptcp.enabled = 1 alone doesn't create one: an application has to open an MPTCP socket. We tested both with iproute2 6.1 in a Debian 12 container, where ss -Mlnp listed a test MPTCP listener and skipped a plain TCP one beside it.

How to fix Update the kernel and reboot

Install your distribution's fixed kernel as soon as it ships, then reboot: a kernel update doesn't take effect until the machine boots into it. Reboot container hosts and Kubernetes nodes too. Appliances and cloud images that bundle a kernel need their vendor's update.

On Debian, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and the 15 LTSS releases, Oracle Linux's UEK kernels, and Amazon Linux 2023's kernel6.12 and kernel6.18, the fix is out. On Ubuntu, RHEL, Amazon Linux 2, and Amazon Linux 2023's default kernel, it isn't yet, as of 8:00 PM CDT, October 29. Watch the trackers linked above. Running a self-built kernel? Move to the fixed stable release for its line.

If you can't patch yet

Red Hat publishes no mitigation. The following is Atlas's interim recommendation, based on the CNA's scoring notes, which say the attacking peer supplies IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options in its SYN. TCP traffic almost never carries IPv4 options legitimately, so dropping TCP packets that have them should cost nothing:

ip hdrlength gt 5 matches any IPv4 header longer than the 20-byte minimum, which only options produce. The rule runs before connection tracking and doesn't touch IPv6 or non-TCP traffic. We tested it in a Debian 12 container: it dropped a SYN carrying a Record Route option, and ordinary TCP connections still worked. We haven't tested it against an exploit, and it doesn't fix the kernel. It lasts until reboot, which is fine if the reboot is into a fixed kernel; remove it with nft delete table ip cve_2026_98432. If your edge firewall can drop IPv4 packets with options, doing it there protects every host behind it.

Until then, keep MPTCP listeners off the internet, and put the hosts that have one at the top of the patch list.

Timeline and exploitation status

All times are CDT (UTC−5).

When What Oct 1 · 5:12 PM Eric Dumazet posts the fix, crediting Xinyang Ge of Anthropic as reporter Oct 5 The fix is merged into the kernel's networking tree Oct 11 Linux 7.2.10 and 6.18.56 ship the fix; 7.3-rc7 follows that night Oct 15 · 4:56–7:16 AM Linux 6.12.113, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 5.15.223, and 5.10.272 ship the fix; the CVE record is published at 7:08 AM Oct 16 Oracle publishes UEK errata with the fix for Oracle Linux 7 through 10 Oct 18 Linux 7.3 is released with the fix Oct 24 Amazon Linux 2023's kernel6.18 package is fixed Oct 27 Anthropic's Frontier Red Team describes a remote root exploit for the bug, built by Claude in its lab Oct 29 Ubuntu still lists its kernels as vulnerable; Amazon Linux 2023's kernel6.12 package is fixed; GitHub repositories referencing the CVE appear, one created at 7:22 PM describing a race trigger

Exploitation status. Anthropic says Claude wrote the exploit "after initial prompting," that it runs "arbitrary commands as root, without any credentials or user interaction" on servers with a multipath TCP listener, and that in its proof of concept "it takes 48 minutes to leak a kernel pointer and another five minutes to reach the shell command execution." Anthropic hasn't published the exploit. Its disclosure policy gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before Anthropic discusses details beyond a public advisory. By 8:00 PM CDT on October 29, eight GitHub repositories referenced the CVE. Most describe themselves as audit or mitigation tooling, among them an Ansible role and a livepatch for AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux. One, created at 7:22 PM, says it includes a race trigger. The CVE isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of 8:00 PM CDT. We haven't tested any public proof of concept, and we aren't linking them.

Updates to this post

We'll revise this post and mark it updated when any of these change: fixed kernels from Ubuntu, Red Hat, or Amazon Linux; NVD's analysis; a KEV listing or any report of exploitation; the separate IPv6 fix.

October 29, 8:00 PM CDT: Added Oracle Linux, fixed in its UEK kernels since October 16, and Amazon Linux, fixed in Amazon Linux 2023's 6.12 and 6.18 kernels and pending elsewhere. Eight GitHub repositories now reference the CVE, one describing a race trigger. Ubuntu, Red Hat, Debian, SUSE, NVD, and KEV are unchanged since 11:00 AM, and nothing was corrected. Get help

If the hard part is knowing which hosts, nodes, and appliances run which kernel, and which of them can reboot this week, our advisors can help plan it.

The bug is reachable through any listening TCP port, so it helps to know which ones the internet can see. Our free external audit checks the domains and public IPs you verify for exposed services, publicly visible software versions with known CVEs, TLS, email security, DNS, and HTTP headers.

It's the second Linux kernel fix this month that only takes effect after a reboot. The other, Fragnesia, is being chained with PHP2Shell to get root.

item.title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
item.description:
HackerTube

It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org!

Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews, filtered them down, ran Sonnet over them in a workflow, got rid of spam and low grade content, and narrowed them down to just 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila!

HackerTube:

Contains quality content Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session Keyboard shortcuts Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version

This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 <3.
